appCard.body: A bright, playful learning app for curious little minds. Explore alphabet, numbers, rhymes, spelling, body parts, feelings, opposites, weather, vehicles, shapes, colours, days, months, family and greetings — all in one safe, colourful place. Switch between English, Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, Punjabi and Tamil anytime.
appCard.title: 🌈 Kids Learning World

benefits.body:
✓ Builds letter and number skills early
✓ Grows vocabulary in English and Indian languages
✓ Helps kids name feelings, family and everyday words
✓ Self-paced — no tests, no stress, just joy
✓ Safe for young learners with a grown-up nearby
✓ Designed for ages 3–8
benefits.title: 🎯 Why Kids Love It

features.body:
• Alphabet A–Z with pictures, words and fun facts
• Numbers 1–100 with words and visuals
• Rhymes with sing-along audio
• Spelling in themed word sets
• Body parts and feelings with gentle explanations
• Opposites, weather, seasons and vehicles
• Shapes, colours, days, months, family and greetings
• Tap any card to hear words aloud
• Six languages to explore
features.title: 📚 What You Can Learn

howToUse.body:
1️⃣ Open any colourful card on the home screen
2️⃣ Tap a picture to hear the word and read along
3️⃣ Explore fun facts, try activities and swipe to more items
4️⃣ Press the globe icon to change language
5️⃣ In Rhymes, tap play and sing along!
6️⃣ Take your time — learning should feel like play

offline.title: 📱 Works Offline

bodyParts.description: Tap each picture. Listen, then try to point to that part on your body with a grown-up.

dialog.hint: Where is your {name}? Touch it gently and say the name out loud!

bodyParts.tapAgain: Tap the card on the grid anytime to hear it again.
bodyParts.title: Body parts

head.about: Your head sits on top of your body and holds your brain inside your skull. Your brain helps you think, remember, dream, and learn new things every day. Wearing a helmet when you ride a bike helps keep your head safe.
head.funFact: Did you know? Your brain uses lots of energy even when you rest! Your skull is hard like a helmet to protect your soft brain. Babies have soft spots on their head that grow stronger over time.
head.try: Gently pat your head and say "Head!" Nod yes and shake no. Ask a grown-up why helmets protect your head.

hair.about: Hair grows on top of your head from tiny roots under the skin. It keeps your head a little warmer and can be straight, curly, short, or long. Combing and washing hair keeps it neat and healthy.
hair.funFact: Did you know? Hair grows a tiny bit every day — that is why we cut or comb it! No two people have exactly the same hair. Hair can be black, brown, blonde, red, and more.
hair.try: Touch your hair and say "Hair!" Count how many hair colors you see in your family.

eyes.about: You have two eyes that work together to see the world in color. They blink to stay moist and clean. Your eyes help you read books, watch friends play, and stay safe when you cross a road.
eyes.funFact: Did you know? Your eyes can tell your brain about millions of colors! Tears help wash dust away. Resting your eyes after screen time helps them feel fresh.
eyes.try: Blink ten times slowly. Name three things you see that are your favorite color!

ear.about: You have two ears — one on each side of your head — to catch sounds around you. They help you hear music, friendly voices, warnings, and birds outside. Ears also help you balance when you spin or walk.
ear.funFact: Did you know? Ears keep working while you sleep so you can hear alarms or a parent calling! The shape of your outer ear guides sound inside. Never put sharp things into your ears.
ear.try: Cup your hands behind your ears like shells. What is the quietest sound you can hear?

nose.about: Your nose is in the middle of your face. You breathe through it and smell flowers, food, soap, and rain. Smelling helps you enjoy meals and notice danger such as smoke.
nose.funFact: Did you know? Your nose makes mucus to trap dust and germs — that helps you stay healthy! Smelling yummy food can make you feel hungry. You can breathe through your nose and your mouth.
nose.try: Take a gentle breath in through your nose. Tell a grown-up two things you smell at home.

mouth.about: Your mouth is for eating healthy food, drinking water, talking, and smiling. Lips and teeth inside help you make sounds and chew safely. A kind smile shares happiness with people you love.
mouth.funFact: Did you know? Smiling can help your brain feel happier! Your mouth has many muscles for clear speech. Drinking water keeps your mouth and whole body healthy.
mouth.try: Make your biggest smile and say "Mouth!" Thank someone with a smile today.

teeth.about: Teeth live in your mouth and chop food into small pieces so you can swallow safely. Baby teeth fall out and stronger adult teeth grow in. Brushing twice a day removes germs that cause cavities.
teeth.funFact: Did you know? Children have 20 baby teeth and adults can have up to 32 teeth! The hard enamel on teeth is very strong. Dentists help keep teeth healthy for life.
teeth.try: Show your teeth and pretend to brush every corner for two minutes. Say "Teeth!" when you finish.

tongue.about: Your tongue is a strong muscle inside your mouth. It helps you taste sweet, salty, sour, and bitter foods. It moves food around and helps you say words clearly when you talk.
tongue.funFact: Did you know? Your tongue has thousands of tiny taste buds! It is one of the busiest muscles in your body. The tongue can heal quickly if you bite it by mistake.
tongue.try: Say "Tongue!" and name one sweet food and one sour food you like.

neck.about: Your neck connects your head to your chest. Important tubes inside carry food and air to your stomach and lungs. You can turn your head to look left, right, up, and down.
neck.funFact: Did you know? Giraffes have very long necks! Your voice box sits in your neck area so you can speak and sing. Gentle neck stretches feel good after reading or screens.
neck.try: Slowly turn your head left and right. Say "Neck!" and roll your shoulders once.

shoulders.about: Shoulders are the strong tops of your arms where they meet your body. They help you lift bags, wave hello, and swim in a pool. Shoulder muscles grow stronger when you play active games.
shoulders.funFact: Did you know? Shoulders are among the most flexible joints in your body! Backpacks and jackets rest on them. Warming up shoulders helps before sports and dance.
shoulders.try: Shrug your shoulders up to your ears, then let them drop. Say "Shoulders!" five times.

arm.about: Your arm runs from your shoulder to your elbow and wrist. Arms help you hug family, throw balls, draw pictures, and reach for toys. Bones and muscles work together every time you move your arm.
arm.funFact: Did you know? The funny-bone tingle happens near a nerve at your elbow! Babies often wave their arms before they can walk. Stretching arms feels good after writing or building blocks.
arm.try: Wave hello with one arm, then the other. Say "Arm!" and give yourself a gentle hug.

hand.about: Your hand is at the end of your arm with a palm and five fingers. Hands clap, hold spoons, build towers, and wash with soap and water. Clean hands stop germs from spreading to food and friends.
hand.funFact: Did you know? Each hand has 27 small bones! The fingerprints on your hands are unique — only you have yours. Hands can speak in sign language too.
hand.try: Clap five times. Open and close your hand like a starfish. Say "Hand!"

fingers.about: Fingers are the five parts on each hand. They pick up tiny beads, point at pictures, and press piano keys. Your thumb bends in a special way to touch the other fingers — that helps you grip things.
fingers.funFact: Did you know? Fingerprints help identify people because no two match! Muscles in your arm pull your fingers with long tendons. Trimming nails keeps germs away.
fingers.try: Wiggle each finger one by one and count to five. Touch your thumb to every fingertip.

leg.about: Legs are the strong limbs from your hips to your feet that hold your body up. You walk, run, jump, and dance with your legs. Leg muscles need exercise, stretching, and rest to stay healthy.
leg.funFact: Did you know? The femur in your leg is the longest and strongest bone in your body! Your legs carry your whole weight all day long. Kangaroos have powerful back legs for hopping.
leg.try: March in place: left, right, left, right. Say "Leg!" and stretch one leg behind you while holding a chair.

knee.about: Your knee is the joint in the middle of your leg where it bends. Knees let you sit on the floor, squat to pick up toys, and climb stairs. Soft padding inside cushions the bones when you move.
knee.funFact: Did you know? You need bent knees to walk smoothly! Knees bend and straighten thousands of times each day. A mat protects them when you kneel on the floor.
knee.try: Bend both knees slowly, then stand tall. Say "Knee!" and sit cross-legged gently.

foot.about: Your foot is at the bottom of your leg with a heel, arch, and toes. Feet balance your whole body when you stand and push off the ground when you walk or run. Shoes protect feet from sharp or hot surfaces.
foot.funFact: Did you know? About one quarter of all the bones in your body are in your feet! Socks and shoes keep feet comfy. Your left and right feet are usually a little different in size.
foot.try: Stomp one foot gently, then the other. Say "Foot!" and wiggle all your toes.

toes.about: Toes are the five small parts on each foot. They help you balance on tiptoes and push when you run or swim. Toenails protect the tips like little shields.
toes.funFact: Did you know? You have ten toes in total — five on each foot! Toes help swimmers push off the pool wall. Wiggling toes often makes people giggle!
toes.try: Wiggle all ten toes inside your socks. Count them with a grown-up from 1 to 10!

emotions.description: All feelings are normal. Tap a face to hear the word — try saying it with a grown-up you trust.

dialog.hint: This feeling is called {name}. Every child feels many things — that is how we grow.

emotions.tapAgain: Close and tap the same card to hear the word again.
emotions.title: Feelings

happy.about: Happy feels warm and sunny inside your chest! You might smile, laugh, clap, or want to jump and play. Happy feelings help your body feel light and your brain remember good moments.
happy.funFact: Did you know? Smiling can help your body feel calmer, even if you start with a tiny smile! Thinking about people you love can bring happy feelings back.
happy.try: Name three things that make you happy. Say them out loud, then draw a little sunshine!

sad.about: Sad can feel heavy, like a rainy day inside. It is okay to cry, rest, or want a hug when you feel sad. Sad feelings often mean you care about something important.
sad.funFact: Did you know? Tears help wash your eyes and can show grown-ups you need comfort! Feeling sad sometimes is normal for every child.
sad.try: If you feel sad, tell a grown-up you trust. Hug a soft toy and say “I feel sad” — that is brave and helpful.

angry.about: Angry can feel hot and strong in your body. Your heart might beat fast and your hands might want to squeeze. It is a normal feeling when something feels unfair or too hard.
angry.funFact: Did you know? Slow breaths can help angry feelings shrink, like a balloon losing air! Moving to a quiet spot can help your body cool down safely.
angry.try: Pretend to blow out birthday candles slowly — breathe in … breathe out … three times. Tell a grown-up what made you angry.

scared.about: Scared can happen when something feels new, big, or loud. Your body is trying to keep you safe — that is its job! Scared feelings usually pass when you feel safe with someone you trust.
scared.funFact: Did you know? Even brave firefighters and doctors feel scared sometimes — they still do kind, safe things! Your brain learns what is safe over time.
scared.try: Hold a stuffed toy or pillow. With a grown-up nearby, say “I am safe” three times in a calm voice.

surprised.about: Surprised is when something unexpected happens — your eyes go wide, your mouth might open, and you might say “Wow!” or “Oh!” It can feel exciting or a little shocking.
surprised.funFact: Did you know? Surprises can be fun (like a birthday cake) or startling (like a loud bang)! Your body needs a moment to understand what happened.
surprised.try: Cover your mouth with your hands and say “Oh!” like a surprised face. Tell someone what surprised you today.

shy.about: Shy means you feel quiet or small around new people or big groups. Many kids feel shy — it does not mean something is wrong with you. Shy feelings often fade as you get to know people.
shy.funFact: Did you know? Shy kids often notice kind little details that others miss! Being shy can also mean you think before you speak — that is a strength.
shy.try: Wave a small hello with one hand if you feel shy today. Practice saying your name to one friendly face.

proud.about: Proud feels like a gold star glowing in your chest! You might feel proud when you tried something hard, shared nicely, or helped someone. Pride can come from effort, not only from winning.
proud.funFact: Did you know? Being proud of trying helps your brain want to learn more! Grown-ups feel proud of you for kind tries, not only perfect scores.
proud.try: Tell someone one thing you did well today — even if it was small. Stand tall and say “I am proud of my try!”

tired.about: Tired means your body and brain need rest. Yawning, heavy eyes, slow moves, and wanting to lie down are clues. Rest helps you grow strong and think clearly tomorrow.
tired.funFact: Did you know? Sleep helps your brain store memories from the day — like saving a game! Even short quiet time can help tired feelings.
tired.try: Yawn big like a sleepy lion. Stretch your arms up, then tell a grown-up if you need a nap or bedtime soon.

excited.about: Excited feels bubbly and fizzy — like you cannot wait! Birthdays, trips, parties, or meeting a friend can feel exciting. Your body might wiggle because it has extra energy.
excited.funFact: Did you know? Excited feelings can make your heart beat faster, just like running! It helps to take a breath before you rush or shout.
excited.try: Jump gently three times and whisper what you are excited about. Draw one picture of the fun thing coming soon!

calm.about: Calm feels peaceful and quiet inside, like sitting on soft grass or listening to gentle music. When you are calm, your muscles relax and your mind can notice small sounds around you.
calm.funFact: Did you know? Calm bodies breathe slowly and deeply! Animals like cats and turtles rest when they feel calm — you can learn from them.
calm.try: Sit still for five slow breaths. Watch your tummy move in and out like a gentle wave.

worried.about: Worried is when your mind keeps thinking “What if?” about something that might happen. Your tummy might feel fluttery. Many kids feel worried — it does not mean bad things will happen.
worried.funFact: Did you know? Talking about worries with a grown-up can make them feel smaller, like sharing a heavy backpack! Writing worries down can help too.
worried.try: Draw your worry on paper, then crumple it and toss it gently into a basket. Tell a grown-up one worry and one hope.

silly.about: Silly feels goofy and playful — funny faces, silly walks, made-up words, and giggles that bubble up! Being silly with safe friends can help stress melt away.
silly.funFact: Did you know? Laughing is good exercise for your face and tummy muscles! A little silly time can turn a grumpy mood into a sunny one.
silly.try: Make the silliest face you can without making a sound! Show it to a grown-up and see if they giggle too.

loved.about: Loved feels warm, safe, and special — like a big hug from someone who cares about you. You can feel loved by family, friends, teachers, or pets who show they care.
loved.funFact: Did you know? Love can be shown with kind words, hugs, helping, listening, and spending time together! Your heart can feel loved even when people are far away.
loved.try: Give yourself a gentle hug and say “I am loved.” Tell someone one reason you feel loved today.

lonely.about: Lonely is when you wish someone were near to play, talk, or sit with you. It can happen even in a busy room. Lonely feelings show you want connection — that is important.
lonely.funFact: Did you know? Even one kind friend, a pet, or a phone call can soften lonely feelings! Telling a grown-up is a strong and smart step.
lonely.try: Tell a grown-up “I feel lonely.” Ask to call a friend, read together, or draw a picture of who you miss.

bored.about: Bored is when nothing feels fun right now and time feels slow. Your brain is asking for something new to explore. Bored does not last forever — ideas can pop up!
bored.funFact: Did you know? Bored time can spark creative ideas — like building, drawing, or inventing a game! Many inventors got ideas when they felt bored first.
bored.try: Name three things you could try: draw, dance, or build with blocks. Pick one and try it for five minutes.

curious.about: Curious means your brain wants to know “Why?” and “How?” — like a little scientist with bright eyes! You might peek, ask questions, or want to touch and learn.
curious.funFact: Did you know? Curious kids ask great questions — that is how people discover animals, stars, and new foods! Grown-ups love thoughtful questions.
curious.try: Point at something nearby and ask one question about it. Write or draw what you wonder.

brave.about: Brave does not mean never scared — it means trying something kind or important even when you feel a little afraid. You can be brave in small steps, like saying hello or trying again.
brave.funFact: Did you know? Firefighters, doctors, and teachers practice being brave to help others! Every brave try makes your confidence grow a little.
brave.try: Stand tall like a superhero for three seconds and say “I can try!” Tell a grown-up one brave thing you did.

kind.about: Kind means you care about others’ feelings — sharing, helping, listening, or saying gentle words. Kindness can be as small as letting someone go first on the slide.
kind.funFact: Did you know? One kind act can start a chain — your friend might be kind back! Kindness helps classrooms and families feel safe.
kind.try: Do one tiny kind thing today: share, help carry something, or say thank you. Notice how it feels in your chest.

confused.about: Confused is when something does not make sense yet — like a puzzle with missing pieces. Your brain is working hard! It is okay to feel confused; asking questions is smart.
confused.funFact: Did you know? Teachers love good questions — confusion often means you are learning something brand new! Even grown-ups feel confused sometimes.
confused.try: Raise your hand or tell a grown-up: “Can you explain again, please?” Draw a question mark on paper.

grateful.about: Grateful means thankful — you notice good things like food, friends, sunshine, or a cozy bed. Gratitude helps your heart focus on what you have, not only what you want.
grateful.funFact: Did you know? Saying thank you helps your brain spot more good things each day! Grateful feelings can grow when you share them out loud.
grateful.try: Name three things you are thankful for today. Say thank you to someone who helped you.

nervous.about: Nervous can feel fluttery in your tummy before a test, a show, or meeting new people. Your body is getting ready to do something important. Nervous and excited can feel similar!
nervous.funFact: Did you know? Many singers and athletes feel nervous before they perform — then they do amazing things! Breathing slowly tells your body you are safe.
nervous.try: Squeeze your hands tight, then open them wide and breathe out slowly. Tell a grown-up one thing that makes you nervous.

jealous.about: A little jealous can happen when you wish you had what someone else has — a toy, skill, or attention. Many kids feel this. Jealousy often means you care about something that matters to you.
jealous.funFact: Did you know? Talking about jealous feelings with a grown-up helps them shrink! You are special in your own way, with your own strengths.
jealous.try: Tell a grown-up how you feel. Name one thing you are good at and one thing you are glad a friend has.

playful.about: Playful means your body and mind are ready for fun — games, tag, pretend play, jokes, and wiggles! Play helps you learn social skills and use extra energy in a happy way.
playful.funFact: Did you know? Play helps your brain build strong connections for learning and friendship! Animals play too — puppies and kittens practice with play fights.
playful.try: Hop like a bunny three times and giggle! Invite someone to play one short game with clear rules.

grumpy.about: Grumpy feels cranky and prickly — little things might bother you more than usual. Often your body needs food, water, rest, or a quiet break. Grumpy feelings usually pass.
grumpy.funFact: Did you know? A healthy snack, a drink of water, or ten minutes of quiet time often helps grumpy moods! Even grown-ups get grumpy when they are tired.
grumpy.try: Take three slow breaths. Tell a grown-up what your body might need: snack, nap, hug, or break.

hopeful.about: Hopeful means you believe good things can happen — like waiting for a fun day, a visit, or fixing a problem. Hope keeps your heart looking forward instead of giving up.
hopeful.funFact: Did you know? Hope helps people keep trying when something is hard! Planting a seed is hopeful — you trust it can grow with care.
hopeful.try: Close your eyes and picture one good thing that might happen tomorrow. Draw or tell someone about your hope.

relieved.about: Relieved is a big “Phew!” when worry or tension goes away — like after finding a lost toy or finishing something scary. Your shoulders and tummy might feel lighter.
relieved.funFact: Did you know? Your shoulders often drop down when you feel relieved! Your body was holding tight, then it can relax.
relieved.try: Say “Phew!” out loud and shake your hands loose like dripping water. Tell someone what worry just ended.

embarrassed.about: Embarrassed can feel hot in your cheeks when something silly or unexpected happens in front of others. You might want to hide. Everyone makes mistakes — it does not mean you are bad.
embarrassed.funFact: Did you know? Grown-ups feel embarrassed too, and it usually passes quickly! Kind friends forget small silly moments fast.
embarrassed.try: Take one deep breath. Tell yourself “I am still loved.” Share the story with a trusted grown-up if you want.

yucky.about: Yucky (grossed out) is when something smells, looks, tastes, or feels unpleasant to you. Your brain and nose are saying “Stay away — that might not be safe or clean!”
yucky.funFact: Did you know? Your nose and brain work as a team to protect you — like a warning sign! It is okay to say no thank you to food you do not trust.
yucky.try: Pinch your nose gently and make a funny “Eww!” face — then laugh with a friend. Wash hands if something was dirty.

missYou.about: Missing someone means you love them and wish they were here right now — maybe they traveled, moved, or you are apart for a while. Missing shows your heart cares deeply.
missYou.funFact: Did you know? Photos, phone calls, voice messages, or drawing a picture can help when you miss someone! Telling them “I miss you” is a loving gift.
missYou.try: Draw a heart and say their name. Tell a grown-up you miss them — maybe you can call or write a note.

disappointed.about: Disappointed is when you hoped for something and it did not happen — a game, plan, or treat. That hurts a little inside. It is okay to feel disappointed; your hope mattered.
disappointed.funFact: Did you know? A hug, talk, or new plan can help disappointed feelings soften! Many kids try again another day and feel proud later.
disappointed.try: Tell a grown-up what you wished for. Ask if there is another day to try, or choose one small fun thing to do now.

numbers.description: Tap a number to see how it looks in words.

dialog.explain: This is how we write number {value} in words.

numbers.title: Numbers {range}

1.about: One means a single thing - one sun, one moon, one nose. It is the first step in counting.
1.funFact: Did you know? The number one can stand for "only one" or "number one" as best effort in games.
1.try: Show one finger up and say "{name}!"

2.about: Two means a pair - like two eyes, two ears, or two shoes. Pairs help us compare and match things.
2.funFact: Did you know? Many body parts come in twos, which helps with balance and direction.

3.about: Three comes after two. Triangles have three sides, and stories often use groups of three.
3.funFact: Did you know? Morning, afternoon, and night are three main parts of a day.
3.try: Tap your knee 3 times and say "{name}!"

4.about: Four is a stable number. Many tables have four legs, and squares have four equal sides.
4.funFact: Did you know? Most cars and many animals move using four points touching the ground.
4.try: March 4 steps in place and say "{name}!"

5.about: Five is the number of fingers on one hand. It is easy to count with five using your hand.
5.funFact: Did you know? Star drawings often use five points, making five easy to remember.
5.try: Spread one hand wide and say "{name}!"

6.about: Six is one more than five. It can be seen in groups like six crayons or six blocks.
6.funFact: Did you know? A honeybee has six legs - three on each side.
6.try: Count to 6 while touching six different objects nearby.

7.about: Seven comes after six and is a favorite number in many stories and songs.
7.funFact: Did you know? A week has seven days from Monday to Sunday.
7.try: Say the days of the week and stop at seven.

8.about: Eight is made of two groups of four. It is a bigger number that still feels easy to group.
8.funFact: Did you know? An octopus has eight arms, so eight is linked to sea life.
8.try: Draw an 8 in the air and say "{name}!"

9.about: Nine is one less than ten. It is close to a full set of ten, so it helps in number comparisons.
9.funFact: Did you know? Multiples of nine make fun finger tricks in math practice.
9.try: Count from 1 to 9 slowly with fingers.

10.about: Ten is a big milestone in early counting. It means two full hands of fingers together.
10.funFact: Did you know? Many counting systems use groups of ten to build larger numbers.
10.try: Show both hands and say "{name}!" proudly.

11.about: Eleven is the first number after ten. It starts the teen journey with special number words.
11.funFact: Did you know? Eleven is made of one ten and one extra one.
11.try: Say "{name}" and then say: ten plus one.

12.about: Twelve is a dozen. We see twelve in clocks and in the twelve months of a year.
12.funFact: Did you know? Eggs are often sold in a dozen, which means twelve.
12.try: Pretend to point around a clock and stop at 12.

13.about: Thirteen comes after twelve and begins bigger teen counting.
13.funFact: Did you know? Thirteen is ten plus three.
13.try: Say "{name}" and show ten fingers plus three fingers.

20.about: Twenty means two groups of ten. It is an important jump from small numbers to bigger counting.
20.funFact: Did you know? Counting by tens makes it easy to reach twenty quickly: 10, 20.
20.try: Clap 2 big claps for two tens and say "{name}!"

50.about: Fifty is halfway to one hundred. It is five groups of ten.
50.funFact: Did you know? Half of 100 is 50, so fifty is the middle marker to a hundred.
50.try: Say "{name}" and draw a big 5 then 0 in the air.

100.about: One hundred is ten groups of ten. It is a proud milestone in number learning.
100.funFact: Did you know? 100 is called a century when we count years.
100.try: Cheer loudly: "{name}!" and do a tiny celebration dance.

detail.odd: Odd number — one friend waits in a pair!
detail.position: You are at {value} on the path to 100 — only {left} more to go!

ten.about: Ten is a strong base number. {value} means {name} - both hands full of fingers.
ten.funFact: Did you know? Many games start with counting to ten before action begins.
ten.try: Count 1 to 10 on fingers and say each number clearly.

teen.about: {name} is a teen number between ten and twenty. Teen numbers mix one ten with extra ones.
teen.funFact: Did you know? Numbers 13 to 19 often end with "teen," which hints at ten plus something.
teen.try: Say "{name}" and split it as ten + ones.

roundTen.about: {name} is a round tens number at {value}. Round tens help children count faster in jumps.
roundTen.funFact: Did you know? 20, 30, 40 and other round tens are easy checkpoints on the path to 100.
roundTen.try: Count by tens up to {value} in a steady rhythm.

compound.about: {name} is {value}. It is built by combining {tensName} and {onesName}.
compound.funFact: Did you know? Breaking compound numbers into tens and ones makes mental math easier.

hundred.about: {name} is {value}, the largest number in this learning set. It means ten tens together.
hundred.funFact: Did you know? Reaching 100 shows strong counting practice and number confidence.
hundred.try: Count by tens to 100 with a grown-up and celebrate at the end.

funFacts.0: Imagine {value} bright stars twinkling just for you tonight.
funFacts.1: At {value}, you can focus on one clear goal at a time.
funFacts.2: {value} is perfect for pairs like shoes, socks, or gloves.
funFacts.3: Groups of {value} are common in stories: beginning, middle, and end.
funFacts.4: {value} corners make a square - strong and easy to spot.
funFacts.5: {value} fingers on one hand help quick counting.
funFacts.6: {value} can be split as 3 + 3, a balanced group.
funFacts.7: A full week has {value} days - a complete cycle.
funFacts.8: {value} can be seen as two sets of 4.
funFacts.9: {value} is just one step before ten.
funFacts.11: {value} starts numbers beyond ten with confidence.

tries.0: Trace {value} in the air and say its name slowly.
tries.2: Touch {num} objects and count each one.
tries.3: Draw {num} small dots and count them.
tries.4: Clap {num} times in a steady beat.
tries.5: Tap each finger on one hand while counting to {num}.
tries.6: March {num} steps and say each count aloud.
tries.7: Balance for {num} seconds with a grown-up nearby.
tries.9: Count down from {value} to 1 like a mini rocket.
tries.10: Say "{name}" and show two full hands.
tries.11: Say ten, then add one more: {name}.

opposites.description: Each card shows two opposite ideas. Tap to hear both words — say them out loud with a grown-up.

dialog.hint: These two are opposites! Say: {first} ∦ then ∦ {second}.

opposites.tapAgain: Tap any card on the grid to hear the pair again.
opposites.title: Opposites

bigSmall.about: {first} means large in size, while {second} means little in size. An elephant is {first}, and a ladybug is {second}. A beach ball can look {first} beside a marble. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare size.
bigSmall.funFact: Blue whales are the largest animals on Earth, but tiny ants can carry food many times their own weight. Seeds come in many sizes, from small poppy seeds to big coconuts. Comparing size helps builders choose the right boxes and tools.
bigSmall.try: Find a {first} safe object and a {second} safe object at home, such as a pillow and a button. Put them side by side and describe how they are different. Ask an adult before picking up anything heavy.

hotCold.about: {first} means having a high temperature, while {second} means having a low temperature. Soup can be {first}, and ice cream is {second}. The sun can make the sidewalk feel {first}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare temperature.
hotCold.funFact: Penguins stay warm with layers of feathers and fat in very cold places. Water can turn into ice when it gets cold enough. Adults test bath water so it is safe and comfortable.
hotCold.try: With an adult, touch the outside of a cup of cold water and a cup of warm, not {first}, water. Describe how each cup feels. Never touch ovens, kettles, or very {first} food without an adult.

dayNight.about: {first} is the bright time when the sun is up, while {second} is the dark time after the sun goes down. We often play and learn during {first}. We often rest during {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare times of day.
dayNight.funFact: Earth spins, which makes places move from daylight into darkness. Some animals, such as owls, are active at night. Streetlights and reflectors help people be seen when it is dark.
dayNight.try: Draw one picture of things you do in {first} and another of things you do in {second}. Look outside with an adult and notice the sky colors. Name one animal that may be awake at night.

happySad.about: {first} is a feeling of joy or pleasure, while {second} is a feeling of unhappiness or hurt. You may feel {first} when playing with a friend. You may feel {second} when a favorite toy breaks. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare feelings.
happySad.funFact: Feelings can change during a day, and all feelings are okay to talk about. Faces, voices, and body language can give clues about how someone feels. Sharing feelings with a trusted adult can help.
happySad.try: Make a {first} face and a {second} face in a mirror. Draw colors or pictures for each feeling. Tell a trusted adult about a time you felt each one.

fastSlow.about: {first} means moving quickly from one place to another. {second} means moving at a lower speed and taking more time. A cheetah can run {first}, while a tortoise moves {second}. {first} and {second} are opposite words that help us compare how things move.
fastSlow.funFact: Different animals move at different speeds. Some vehicles, like trains and airplanes, can travel very fast. Walking slowly helps us stay careful and balanced in crowded places. We use these words every day to describe movement and speed.
fastSlow.try: Walk {second} across the room and notice how long it takes. Now walk {first} and compare the time. Watch a bird and a snail, or a bicycle and a person walking. Can you identify which one is {first} and which one is {second}?

tallShort.about: {first} means having a greater height, while {second} means having less height. A giraffe is {first}, and a puppy may be {second}. A {first} tree can reach high above a house. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare height.
tallShort.funFact: Plants can grow taller when they get sunlight, water, and care. People grow at different rates and heights. Measuring height helps doctors check how children are growing.
tallShort.try: Stand beside a trusted adult and compare your heights. Build a {first} tower and a {second} tower with blocks. Keep blocks on the floor so the towers stay safe.

upDown.about: {first} means toward a higher place, while {second} means toward a lower place. A balloon can float {first}, and a ball can roll {second} a hill. Your hands move {first} when you reach for a shelf. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare direction.
upDown.funFact: Birds use their wings to move up into the air and down to land. Elevators carry people up and down in tall buildings. Looking where you are going helps you use stairs safely.
upDown.try: Point {first} to the ceiling and {second} to the floor. Roll a ball gently down a ramp. With an adult nearby, walk up and down a few stairs while holding the handrail.

fullEmpty.about: {first} means holding as much as it can, while {second} means holding nothing inside. A cup of water can be {first}. A bowl after all the cereal is eaten can be {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare how much something holds.
fullEmpty.funFact: A measuring cup shows how much liquid is inside. Birds fill nests with soft materials before laying eggs. Empty containers can often be reused or recycled.
fullEmpty.try: With an adult, fill a small cup with water, then pour it back until the cup is {second}. Compare the two cups. Wipe up any spills so no one slips.

cleanDirty.about: {first} means free from dirt, while {second} means covered with dirt or mess. Washed hands are {first}. Shoes after a muddy walk may be {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare how things look and feel.
cleanDirty.funFact: Washing hands with soap helps remove germs that can make us sick. Farmers often get dirty while growing food. Keeping toys clean helps everyone enjoy them safely.
cleanDirty.try: Use soap and water to wash your hands with an adult's reminder. Compare a clean plate with a dirty plate before washing. Help put a dirty towel into the laundry basket.

loudQuiet.about: {first} means making a strong sound, while {second} means making little or no sound. A fire truck siren is {first}. A library is usually {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare sounds.
loudQuiet.funFact: Our ears help us hear sounds, so they need protection from very loud noises. Many animals use quiet sounds to communicate. Quiet voices can help other people concentrate or rest.
loudQuiet.try: Clap once loudly, then tap your fingers quietly. Listen for three quiet sounds in your room. Use a quiet voice near a sleeping person or baby.

openClosed.about: {first} means not shut so something can enter or leave, while {second} means shut. A door can be {first} for a guest. A lunch box can be {second} to keep food inside. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare positions.
openClosed.funFact: Flowers can open in sunlight and close at another time of day. Closed gates can keep children and pets safe. Some jars need to stay closed so food stays fresh.
openClosed.try: With permission, open and close a book or a safe box. Sort pictures of things that are open and closed. Ask an adult before opening doors, windows, or containers.

lightDark.about: {first} means having brightness so we can see, while {second} means having little or no brightness. A lamp makes a room {first}. A room with the lights off can be {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare brightness.
lightDark.funFact: The Moon reflects light from the Sun. Our eyes need time to adjust when we move from light to dark. Reflective strips on bags and bicycles help people be seen at night.
lightDark.try: With an adult, turn a lamp on and off and notice the difference. Look for {first} and {second} colors in a picture. Do not stare at the Sun or shine lights into anyone's eyes.

goodBad.about: {first} can mean helpful, kind, or working well, while {second} can mean harmful, unkind, or not working well. Sharing can be a {first} choice. Hurting someone is a {second} choice. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare choices and results.
goodBad.funFact: Rules help people make safe and caring choices. A mistake does not make someone bad; mistakes can teach us what to do next time. Saying sorry and fixing a problem can be helpful.
goodBad.try: Think of one {first} choice you can make today, such as putting toys away. Act out asking before borrowing something. Talk with an adult about how to fix a small mistake.

nearFar.about: {first} means close by, while {second} means a long distance away. Your shoes may be {first} your bed. A mountain may look {second} from your window. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare distance.
nearFar.funFact: Maps show places that are near and far from one another. Sound can seem quieter when it comes from far away. Staying near a trusted adult is important in busy places.
nearFar.try: Place one toy near you and another farther away. Take small steps to the farther toy and count them. When outdoors, stay near your adult and ask before going anywhere.

youngOld.about: {first} means having lived for a short time, while {second} means having lived for a long time. A baby is {first}, and a grandparent is {second}. A tree may be {first} when it has grown for only a few years. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare age.
youngOld.funFact: Some turtles can live for many decades. Tree rings can give clues about how old a tree is. Older people can share stories and skills they have learned.
youngOld.try: Look at family photos with an adult and notice how people change as they grow. Draw a {first} plant and an {second} tree. Ask an older family member to share a childhood memory.

softHard.about: {first} means easy to press or bend, while {second} means firm and difficult to press. A pillow is {first}, and a rock is {second}. A sponge feels {first} when you squeeze it. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare how things feel.
softHard.funFact: Many animals have soft fur or feathers to help keep them warm. Hard shells protect some animals, such as turtles. Builders choose hard materials for strong walls and roads.
softHard.try: Touch safe objects such as a cotton ball and a wooden block. Sort them into {first} and {second} groups. Ask an adult before touching anything sharp or breakable.

sweetSour.about: {first} is a sugary taste, while {second} is a sharp, tangy taste. A ripe banana can taste {first}. A lemon can taste {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare flavors.
sweetSour.funFact: Taste buds on our tongues help us notice flavors. Fruits can taste different as they ripen. Brushing teeth after sweets helps keep teeth healthy.
sweetSour.try: With an adult, taste a small piece of banana and a tiny piece of lemon if it is safe for you. Describe the flavors. Drink water afterward and brush your teeth at the usual time.

wetDry.about: {first} means covered with water or another liquid, while {second} means not wet. Rain can make the grass {first}. A towel can make your hands {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare moisture.
wetDry.funFact: Plants need water, but too much water can flood the ground. Ducks have feathers that help water roll off. Drying hands after washing can help keep them comfortable.
wetDry.try: Dip one corner of a cloth in water and leave another corner dry. Feel the difference. Ask an adult to help clean up water so the floor does not become slippery.

thickThin.about: {first} means wide from one side to the other, while {second} means narrow from one side to the other. A {first} book has many pages. A {second} sheet of paper has little depth. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare width or depth.
thickThin.funFact: Elephants have thick skin that helps protect them. Thin ice can break easily, so people should never walk on it. Artists use thick and thin lines in drawings.
thickThin.try: Compare a thick crayon with a thin pencil. Draw one thick line and one thin line on paper. Ask an adult before handling tools that are not made for children.

heavyLight.about: {first} means weighing a lot, while {second} means weighing a little. A backpack full of books can be {first}. A feather is {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare weight.
heavyLight.funFact: Gravity pulls everything toward Earth. A boat can carry heavy things because its shape helps it float. People use scales to measure weight.
heavyLight.try: Hold a {second} leaf and a {first} book one at a time with an adult's permission. Guess which weighs more, then compare. Never lift anything too difficult for you.

startEnd.about: {first} means the beginning of something, while {second} means when it is finished. The first page is the {first} of a story. The last page is the {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare order.
startEnd.funFact: Races have a start line and a finish line. Recipes have steps that begin with getting ingredients and end with eating or serving. Following steps in order can make tasks easier.
startEnd.try: Tell an adult the start and end of your morning routine. Line up three picture cards from start to end. Begin a short drawing and decide when it is finished.

frontBack.about: {first} means the side or part that faces forward, while {second} means the side or part behind it. A car has headlights at the {first} and taillights at the {second}. Your face is at the {first} of your head. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare position.
frontBack.funFact: Many animals have eyes near the front of their heads to see where they are going. Backpacks are worn on our backs. Knowing front and back helps people give directions safely.
frontBack.try: Point to the front and back of a toy car. Put a sticker on the front of a paper and draw a shape on the back. With an adult, practice saying where an object is.

insideOutside.about: {first} means in or within something, while {second} means not in it. A toy can be {first} a box. A bird can be {second} its nest. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare location.
insideOutside.funFact: People often go inside when storms make outdoor play unsafe. Seeds grow inside fruits. Looking both ways before going outside near roads helps keep everyone safe.
insideOutside.try: Put a soft toy inside a basket, then outside the basket. Tell an adult where it is each time. Look for something inside your room and something outside a window.

winLose.about: {first} means doing best in a game or reaching a goal, while {second} means not winning that time. A team may {first} a match. Another team may {second}, but both can learn and have fun. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare game results.
winLose.funFact: Practice helps people improve skills whether they win or lose. Games have rules so everyone can play fairly. Congratulating others shows kindness.
winLose.try: Play a simple game with a family member. Say kind words whether you win or lose. Talk about one thing you enjoyed and one skill you can practice.

giveTake.about: {first} means handing something to someone, while {second} means receiving or picking something up. You can {first} a card to a friend. You can {second} a turn after someone offers it. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare actions with objects.
giveTake.funFact: Taking turns helps everyone get a chance to play. Giving can be a way to share, help, or show care. We should ask before taking something that belongs to another person.
giveTake.try: Practice giving a soft toy to an adult and taking it back when they offer it. Say “please” and “thank you.” Ask permission before taking any real object.

pushPull.about: {first} means moving something away from you, while {second} means bringing something toward you. You {first} a door to close it. You {second} a wagon toward you. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare forces.
pushPull.funFact: A swing moves because it is pushed. Magnets can pull some metals without touching them. Using both hands and moving slowly can help when opening a heavy door.
pushPull.try: Push a toy car gently away on the floor, then pull it back with a string. Try pushing and pulling a chair only with an adult's permission. Keep fingers away from doors.

highLow.about: {first} means at a greater level or height, while {second} means at a smaller level or height. A bird can fly {first} in the sky. A pebble can lie {second} on the ground. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare position.
highLow.funFact: Mountains are high landforms, while valleys are lower areas between hills. Smoke alarms are placed high because smoke rises. Climbing high places without an adult can be unsafe.
highLow.try: Hold a scarf high above your head, then low near your knees. Place a toy on a low table and notice a high shelf with an adult. Do not climb furniture to reach things.

moreLess.about: {first} means a greater amount, while {second} means a smaller amount. Five apples are {first} than two apples. A cup with one cracker has {second} food than a plate with several crackers. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare amounts.
moreLess.funFact: Counting helps us tell whether there are more or less things. Recipes may need more or less of an ingredient. Sharing can help make sure everyone has enough.
moreLess.try: Make two groups of safe objects, with more in one group and less in the other. Count each group aloud. Ask an adult before using any food or small items.

sameDifferent.about: {first} means alike in an important way, while {second} means not alike. Two red balls can be {first} in color. A ball and a book are {second} shapes. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare things.
sameDifferent.funFact: Leaves from one tree can look similar but still have small differences. People can have different names, abilities, and favorite things. Noticing differences can help us learn about the world respectfully.
sameDifferent.try: Find two objects that are the same color and two that are different colors. Compare their shapes and sizes. Tell an adult one way each pair is alike or different.

rightWrong.about: {first} means correct or fair, while {second} means not correct or not fair. Following a safety rule can be {first}. Taking someone else's toy without asking is {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare choices and answers.
rightWrong.funFact: Everyone makes wrong answers sometimes while learning. Checking work can help us find and fix mistakes. Asking a trusted adult for help is a good way to learn what is right.
rightWrong.try: Solve a simple puzzle with an adult and check each answer together. Practice asking before you use another person's things. Think of a way to fix a small wrong choice.

leftRight.about: {first} and {second} name two different sides. Your {first} hand is on one side of your body, and your {second} hand is on the other. A shoe belongs on each side. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare direction.
leftRight.funFact: Maps often use left and right to give directions. Many people prefer one hand for drawing or writing, and either preference is okay. Drivers and walkers use directions to travel safely.
leftRight.try: Raise your left hand, then your right hand. Put a sticker on the left side of a paper and a circle on the right side. Practice directions with an adult while staying in a safe place.

prettyPlain.about: {first} can mean pleasing or decorated, while {second} can mean simple without much decoration. A colorful painting may look {first}. A plain paper cup may have no design. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare appearance.
prettyPlain.funFact: People can like different colors and styles. Some animals use bright patterns to warn others, while others use plain colors to hide. Simple objects can still be useful and special.
prettyPlain.try: Decorate one paper with safe crayons and leave another paper plain. Compare the two designs. Tell an adult what you like about each one.

easyHard.about: {first} means not needing much effort, while {second} means needing more effort or practice. A puzzle with two pieces may be {first}. A puzzle with many pieces may be {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare difficulty.
easyHard.funFact: Practice can make a hard skill easier over time. Brains grow stronger when we keep trying and ask for help. Different tasks can feel easy or hard to different people.
easyHard.try: Try an easy task, such as sorting two colors of blocks, then a harder task, such as making a pattern. Notice how practice helps. Ask an adult for help when you need it.

kindMean.about: {first} means caring and helpful, while {second} means hurtful or unkind. Saying something nice is {first}. Calling someone a hurtful name is {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare how we treat others.
kindMean.funFact: Kind actions can help people feel safe and included. Words can affect feelings even when they are spoken quietly. If someone is mean, a trusted adult can help.
kindMean.try: Say one kind thing to a family member. Practice inviting someone to join a game. Tell a trusted adult if you see or hear mean behavior.

braveScared.about: {first} means facing something difficult even when you feel worried, while {second} means feeling afraid. You may feel {first} when trying a new activity with help. You may feel {second} during a loud storm. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare feelings.
braveScared.funFact: Being brave does not mean never feeling scared. Taking slow breaths and talking to a trusted adult can help with scary feelings. Safety rules help us decide when not to try something alone.
braveScared.try: Draw a time you felt brave and a time you felt scared. Practice taking three slow breaths with an adult. Tell a trusted adult whenever something feels unsafe or scary.

awakeAsleep.about: {first} means not sleeping and able to notice things, while {second} means sleeping. You are {first} when you eat breakfast. You are {second} when you rest in bed at night. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare states of rest.
awakeAsleep.funFact: Sleep helps bodies and brains grow and recover. Many animals sleep at different times than people do. A calming bedtime routine can help children get ready to sleep.
awakeAsleep.try: Make a list with an adult of things you do while awake and asleep. Pretend to yawn, stretch, and get ready for bed. Keep screens and exciting games away from bedtime when an adult suggests it.

sharpRound.about: {first} means having a pointed edge or tip, while {second} means curved with no corners. A pencil point can be {first}. A ball is {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare shapes and edges.
sharpRound.funFact: Some animal teeth are sharp for eating certain foods. Wheels are round so they can roll smoothly. Sharp objects can hurt skin, so they need careful adult handling.
sharpRound.try: Find a round ball and draw a sharp-looking triangle on paper. Sort safe pictures by their shapes. Ask an adult before touching scissors, knives, or pointed tools.

smoothRough.about: {first} means even and without bumps, while {second} means uneven or bumpy. A polished table can feel {first}. Tree bark often feels {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare textures.
smoothRough.funFact: Rough tree bark can protect a tree from weather and insects. Smooth ice can be slippery. People use rough surfaces on some paths to help shoes grip.
smoothRough.try: Touch a smooth spoon and a rough towel. Describe each texture with an adult. Avoid touching surfaces that are hot, sharp, or covered in unknown material.

wideNarrow.about: {first} means having a lot of space from side to side, while {second} means having little space from side to side. A {first} road has room for many cars. A {second} path has less room. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare width.
wideNarrow.funFact: Animals choose wide or narrow spaces depending on their size. A wide bridge can carry many people, while a narrow trail may require walking single file. Staying on marked paths helps protect nature.
wideNarrow.try: Make a wide path and a narrow path with tape or blocks on the floor. Walk carefully along each one. Keep the paths clear so nobody trips.

earlyLate.about: {first} means happening before the expected time, while {second} means happening after the expected time. Waking before the alarm can be {first}. Arriving after a class begins can be {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare time.
earlyLate.funFact: Clocks and calendars help families plan when to do things. Being early can give us time to get ready calmly. Sometimes being late happens, and letting an adult know is helpful.
earlyLate.try: With an adult, look at a clock and choose a time for a small task. Prepare your shoes or bag early for tomorrow. Talk about one way to be on time.

comeGo.about: {first} means moving toward a place or person, while {second} means moving away from a place or person. You {first} to an adult when they call you. You {second} home after visiting a park. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare movement.
comeGo.funFact: Birds come and go from nests to find food. People use schedules to know when buses and trains arrive and leave. Children should always tell a trusted adult before going anywhere.
comeGo.try: Play a safe follow-the-leader game with an adult: come closer, then go a few steps away. Use a stuffed animal to show the directions. Stay where your adult can see you.

firstLast.about: {first} means before all others in order, while {second} means after all others. The {first} runner begins at the front of a line. The {second} page comes at the end of a book. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare order.
firstLast.funFact: Days of the week have a first day and a last day in a calendar row. Taking turns means everyone gets a chance, whether they are first or last. Line order can help groups stay organized.
firstLast.try: Line up three toys and name the first and last toy. Put picture cards in order from first to last. Practice waiting calmly for a turn in a game.

strongWeak.about: {first} means having a lot of power, while {second} means having less power. An elephant is {first} enough to move a log. A baby bird may be {second} before it grows. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare power.
strongWeak.funFact: Muscles become stronger when we move our bodies, eat nourishing food, and rest. Ants may look small but can be very strong for their size. Asking for help is smart when something is too heavy.
strongWeak.try: Gently squeeze a soft ball and notice your muscles working. Compare a strong cardboard tube with a weak paper strip. Ask an adult to carry anything heavy.

sunnyRainy.about: {first} describes weather with bright sunshine, while {second} describes weather when rain falls. A {first} day may have clear skies. A {second} day may have puddles. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare weather.
sunnyRainy.funFact: Sunlight helps plants make food. Rain fills rivers and gives water to plants and animals. Clouds can bring shade, rain, or storms, so checking the weather helps families plan.
sunnyRainy.try: Look outside with an adult and describe the weather. Draw one sunny picture and one rainy picture. Wear a hat for sunny weather or a raincoat for rainy weather when an adult chooses.

summerWinter.about: {first} is a warm season in many places, while {second} is a colder season in many places. People may wear light clothes in {first}. People may wear warm coats in {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare seasons.
summerWinter.funFact: Earth's tilted position as it travels around the Sun helps create seasons. Some animals grow thicker fur for winter. Seasons can be different in different parts of the world.
summerWinter.try: Sort clothing pictures into summer and winter groups. Draw an activity you enjoy in each season. Ask an adult which clothes are right for today's weather.

boyGirl.about: {first} and {second} are words some children use to describe themselves. Children may have different bodies, names, clothes, interests, and ways of playing. A child can choose colors, games, and activities they enjoy. {first} and {second} are words that help us describe people respectfully.
boyGirl.funFact: Every child deserves kindness and respect. Toys, colors, sports, and jobs can be enjoyed by children of any gender. Using a person's name and the words they use for themselves is respectful.
boyGirl.try: Draw yourself doing something you enjoy. Name kind things you can say to any child. Ask an adult how to politely learn what name or words someone prefers.

messyNeat.about: {first} means not tidy or organized, while {second} means tidy and in order. Toys scattered on the floor can be {first}. Books lined up on a shelf can be {second}. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare how things are arranged.
messyNeat.funFact: Keeping paths neat helps people avoid tripping. Artists may make a messy-looking workspace while creating something. Putting things back after use helps everyone find them.
messyNeat.try: Choose a small safe area, such as a toy bin, to tidy with an adult. Look at it when it is messy and when it is neat. Put one item back in its place after play.

laughCry.about: {first} means making a happy sound or movement, while {second} means tears may come from the eyes when someone feels hurt, sad, or overwhelmed. People may laugh at something funny. People may cry when they need comfort. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare ways feelings can show.
laughCry.funFact: People can cry for many reasons, including joy, pain, or tiredness. Laughter can help people feel connected. If someone is crying, a caring adult can help them feel safe.
laughCry.try: Read a funny book with an adult and notice if it makes you laugh. Practice asking, “Are you okay?” in a gentle voice. Tell a trusted adult if you or someone else needs comfort.

stopGo.about: {first} means to stop moving, while {second} means to begin moving. A red traffic light tells cars to {first}. A green traffic light tells cars to {second} when it is safe. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare movement.
stopGo.funFact: Traffic lights and crosswalk signs help people travel safely. Drivers must stop for people crossing the road. Children should cross only with a trusted adult and follow their directions.
stopGo.try: Play a stop-and-go game indoors with an adult: freeze for stop and walk for go. Practice stopping before a doorway. Near roads, always stop and wait for your trusted adult.

sittingStanding.about: {first} means resting your body on a chair, floor, or another seat, while {second} means being upright on your feet. You may be {first} while reading. You may be {second} while waiting in line. {first} and {second} are opposites that help us compare body positions.
sittingStanding.funFact: Sitting and standing use different muscles. Taking breaks to move can help bodies feel comfortable. Chairs are safer when all four legs stay on the floor.
sittingStanding.try: With an adult, sit on a sturdy chair, then stand beside it. Notice how your legs feel in each position. Keep both feet on the floor and do not stand on chairs.

shapes.tapColor: Tap a color to say its name.
shapes.tapShape: Tap a shape to say its name.

circle.about: A circle is a round shape with no corners and no straight sides. Wheels, coins, plates, and the sun in drawings often look like circles.
circle.funFact: Did you know? Every point on a circle is the same distance from the center. That is why wheels are circular - they roll smoothly.
circle.try: Draw a big circle in the air with your finger and say "{name}!" Then find one round thing nearby.

square.about: A square has four equal sides and four corners. Floor tiles, window blocks, and some toy boxes are square.
square.funFact: Did you know? If all four sides are equal and all corners are right angles, it is a square. Squares stack neatly.
square.try: Use your finger to draw 4 sides: up, across, down, across. Say "{name}!"

triangle.about: A triangle has three sides and three corners. Pizza slices, road signs, and party flags can look like triangles.
triangle.funFact: Did you know? The strongest bridge frames often use triangles because they hold shape well.
triangle.try: Make a triangle with both hands and say "{name}!" Then count its 3 corners.

rectangle.about: A rectangle has four corners and opposite sides that match in length. Books, doors, notebooks, and phone screens are often rectangles.
rectangle.funFact: Did you know? A rectangle is like a stretched square. Many rooms and tables are rectangle-shaped.
rectangle.try: Trace a rectangle in front of you and say "{name}!" Find one in your room.

diamond.about: A diamond shape looks like a tilted square with four equal sides. Kite patterns and playing card diamonds use this shape.
diamond.funFact: Did you know? The diamond shape is also called a rhombus in math class.
diamond.try: Tilt your square hand-shape and say "{name}!" Draw one like a kite.

cube.about: A cube is a 3D shape with six equal square faces. Dice, toy blocks, and ice cubes are examples of cubes.
cube.funFact: Did you know? A cube has 8 corners and 12 edges. It is a solid shape, not a flat one.
cube.try: Hold an imaginary block in your hands and say "{name}!" Then find a box-like object.

star.about: A star shape has pointed tips and lines that meet at corners. Kids draw stars in sky pictures and celebrations.
star.funFact: Did you know? The stars in space are actually giant balls of hot gas, but we draw them with points.
star.try: Draw a 5-point star in the air and say "{name}!"

heart.about: A heart shape has two rounded tops and a point at the bottom. It is used in art to show love and care.
heart.funFact: Did you know? Real hearts in our body do not look exactly like the heart symbol, but the symbol is easy to recognize.
heart.try: Make a heart with your fingers and say "{name}!" Think of one person you love.

oval.about: An oval is a stretched circle, like an egg shape. Eggs, some mirrors, and race tracks can look oval.
oval.funFact: Did you know? If you press a circle from two sides, it becomes more oval.
oval.try: Draw an egg-like shape in the air and say "{name}!"

box.about: A box shape in this lesson means a square or rectangular frame. Gift boxes, lunch boxes, and storage boxes use this form.
box.funFact: Did you know? Boxes are designed to hold things safely and stack one above another.
box.try: Pretend to open a box lid and say "{name}!" Name one thing you keep in a box.

line.about: A line is a straight path from one point to another. Roads, rulers, and notebook margins use lines.
line.funFact: Did you know? Lines can be horizontal, vertical, or slanting. Shapes are made by joining lines.
line.try: Draw one long straight line with your finger and say "{name}!"

pentagon.about: A pentagon has five sides and five corners. Some badges and building designs use pentagon shapes.
pentagon.funFact: Did you know? If you count carefully, every pentagon always has 5 edges.
pentagon.try: Count 1 to 5 while tracing a pentagon in the air and say "{name}!"

hexagon.about: A hexagon has six sides and six corners. Honeycomb cells made by bees are famous hexagon shapes.
hexagon.funFact: Did you know? Hexagons fit together without gaps, so bees use them to store honey efficiently.
hexagon.try: Pretend to draw a honeycomb cell and say "{name}!" Count 6 sides.

octagon.about: An octagon has eight sides and eight corners. Stop signs in many countries are octagons.
octagon.funFact: Did you know? The word octagon starts with "octa," which means eight.
octagon.try: Hold up 8 fingers while saying "{name}!" Then imagine a stop sign.

cloudShape.about: A cloud shape is soft and puffy with curved bumps. Kids often draw clouds as rounded fluffy forms in the sky.
cloudShape.funFact: Did you know? Real clouds are made of tiny water droplets, but in drawing we use fun cloud outlines.
cloudShape.try: Make a fluffy cloud shape in the air and say "{name}!"

black.about: Black is a very dark color, like night sky without city lights. Blackboards, tires, and some shoes are black.
black.funFact: Did you know? Black absorbs more heat from sunlight than many lighter colors.
black.try: Point to one black object nearby and say "{name}!"

white.about: White is a very light and clean-looking color. Clouds, milk, chalk, and many flowers can be white.
white.funFact: Did you know? White reflects a lot of light, so white clothes can feel cooler in hot sun.
white.try: Find one white thing in the room and say "{name}!"

grey.about: Grey is between black and white. Clouds, stones, and metal objects are often grey.
grey.funFact: Did you know? Mixing black and white paint gives different shades of grey.
grey.try: Show a soft grey color with your pencil or imagine rainy clouds and say "{name}!"

red.about: Red is a bright, warm color seen in apples, roses, and stop signs. It stands out quickly.
red.funFact: Did you know? Red often signals attention, like traffic stop lights and warning signs.
red.try: Name one red fruit and say "{name}!"

orange.about: Orange is a cheerful color between red and yellow. Oranges, marigold flowers, and evening skies can look orange.
orange.funFact: Did you know? Orange is often used for safety cones because it is easy to spot.
orange.try: Pretend to peel an orange fruit and say "{name}!"

yellow.about: Yellow is a bright sunny color. Bananas, lemons, and sunshine drawings are often yellow.
yellow.funFact: Did you know? Yellow is one of the easiest colors to notice from far away.
yellow.try: Draw a tiny sun in the air and say "{name}!"

green.about: Green is the color of many leaves, grass, and plants. It reminds us of nature and fresh growth.
green.funFact: Did you know? Plants look green because of chlorophyll, which helps them make food from sunlight.
green.try: Look for a plant or leaf and say "{name}!"

blue.about: Blue is a calm color often seen in sky and water. Many uniforms, bags, and toys are blue.
blue.funFact: Did you know? Oceans can look blue because water reflects and scatters sunlight.
blue.try: Point up to the sky (or imagine it) and say "{name}!"

skyBlue.about: Sky blue is a light shade of blue, like a clear daytime sky. It feels soft and airy.
skyBlue.funFact: Did you know? Artists use sky blue to paint peaceful weather and open spaces.
skyBlue.try: Spread your arms wide like open sky and say "{name}!"

lightGreen.about: Light green is a fresh shade of green, like new leaves or spring grass. It looks bright and lively.
lightGreen.funFact: Did you know? New plant leaves are often lighter green than old leaves.
lightGreen.try: Imagine tiny new leaves growing and say "{name}!"

darkOrange.about: Dark orange is a deeper shade of orange, like autumn leaves or evening marigolds.
darkOrange.funFact: Did you know? Dark orange is used in signs and sports gear because it remains bold and visible.
darkOrange.try: Pretend to color a pumpkin and say "{name}!"

darkBlue.about: Dark blue is a deeper, richer blue like late evening sky or school uniforms. It feels strong and calm.
darkBlue.funFact: Did you know? Navy blue is a popular dark blue used in uniforms and formal clothes.
darkBlue.try: Close your eyes and imagine night sky, then say "{name}!"

darkGreen.about: Dark green is a deep green shade found in thick forests and big tree leaves.
darkGreen.funFact: Did you know? Dark green shades are often used to show trees and nature in maps and drawings.
darkGreen.try: Pretend to be a tall tree and say "{name}!"

purple.about: Purple is a color made by mixing red and blue. Grapes, lavender flowers, and some dresses can be purple.
purple.funFact: Did you know? In old times, purple dye was rare and expensive, so it was linked with royalty.
purple.try: Name one purple fruit or flower and say "{name}!"

pink.about: Pink is a soft, playful color often seen in flowers, candies, and toys.
pink.funFact: Did you know? Pink is usually made by adding white to red, creating a lighter shade.
pink.try: Draw a tiny pink heart in the air and say "{name}!"

brown.about: Brown is an earthy color seen in tree trunks, soil, chocolate, and wooden furniture.
brown.funFact: Did you know? Many animals use brown fur or feathers to blend into nature.
brown.try: Touch a wooden object or imagine soil and say "{name}!"

gold.about: Gold is a shiny yellow-metal color that looks rich and bright. Trophies, stars, and festive decorations may look gold.
gold.funFact: Did you know? Real gold is a metal that does not rust easily.
gold.try: Pretend to wear a gold crown and say "{name}!"

silver.about: Silver is a cool shiny grey-metal color. Spoons, foil, and some stars in drawings look silver.
silver.funFact: Did you know? Silver is a real metal used in jewelry and special electronics.
silver.try: Pretend to polish a silver spoon and say "{name}!"
